newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britons indifferent to Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britons indifferent to Hong Kong handover.

text.p: With the sun setting on Britain's colonial empire in Hong Kong, the newspaper seller in London's Piccadilly Circus put it bluntly: "There are too many Chinese here already."
Christopher Watson wasn't worried about guaranteeing human rights after the handover to Beijing in July or ensuring Hong Kong remains one of the world's economic success stories.
Even though Britain has offered passports to just 50,000 Hong Kong households in a territory of 6.3 million, he frankly didn't want any more of them over here.
And he was the first to admit that Britons regard the handover -- if they think of it at all -- with a mixture of ignorance and indifference.
It took the death of China's 92-year-old paramount leader Deng Xiaoping to focus minds -- however briefly -- on the issue of Hong Kong.
But even in London's bustling Chinatown, pragmatism reigned.
"China was fortunate to have him but there was no energy left. Everyone must die and surely it was his turn," said 50-year-old shopkeeper Patrick Tsang.

Siu Koon Ho, a 25-year-old tourist from Hong Kong, put it even more bluntly: "For so long we didn't see him except in the same old photos, that I sometimes thought he was dead already and nobody had told us."
HONG KONG NOT AN ELECTION ISSUE

Political parties adopt a bipartisan stance on Hong Kong. It is unlikely to figure large in Britain's forthcoming election. But inevitably there will be concern that any signs of a power struggle in Beijing could spell instability for Hong Kong.
Not everyone is as blunt as the newspaper seller in their reaction to the handover.
But student Duncan Woods agreed that the end of 150 years of colonial rule in Hong Kong and China's plans to roll back civil liberties did not grab the headlines.
"For many people, it is thousands of miles away and all about lots of people that don't affect them. That is a shame."

Peter Njoko, a London underground railway inspector whose parents came to Britain from Nigeria, offered the other side of the coin: "I don't think it is fair that only a limited amount of people can come here. They should have the free right."
HONG KONG FORMULA SEEN LIKELY TO SURVIVE

In Chinatown, the Soho shopkeepers and restaurateurs worried even before Deng's death about China's human rights record after the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown. But they believe Hong Kong can survive as a humming capitalist dynamo.
Peter Wong, born in Hong Kong but brought up in England, said: "In mainland China, human rights are not as good as in Hong Kong. That is one of the things I worry about."
Alan Lai agreed: "I was born in Hong Kong too. The Chinese give me no faith. I don't feet comfortable at them taking it back from the British."
Hong Kong has boasted one of the fastest growing economies in the world over the past decade. China, with a consumer market of 1.2 billion people, wants to maintain the magic formula.
"Hong Kong is a money-making port and China is not going to take that away," said Beng Hua Lee.
INVESTORS CONFIDENT ABOUT HONG KONG FUTURE

But amid all the political "blood and thunder" on both sides of a border that is soon to vanish, investors in Hong Kong take a more hard-nosed a long-term view. Deng's death had long been factored into calculations.
"The Chinese are very keen to preserve the economy. They do not want to kill the goose that laid the golden egg," said Dudley Lord of Axa Equity and Law Investment.
For the communist giant, Hong Kong is still a glittering jewel with its magnificent port, sophisticated infrastructure and financial expertise.

"The Chinese need it because they cannot reinvent it overnight. It is still the gateway into their southern provinces and always will be," said Richard Murckart, investment director at Edinburgh Fund Managers.

Investors like Richard Farrell of Guinness Flight Global Management argue that geography is the best insurance policy for Hong Kong, gateway to Chinese industries that boast low wages and low real estate costs.

"If the Chinese were to ring up (Governor) Chris Patten and say 'We were only joking, you can keep Hong Kong,' nothing would change. It is all about supervising the manufacturing process in southern China and acting as its shipping agent. The profits you can make in doing that are enormous," he said.
